title: The Assembly Speaks
narrative: The National Assembly has convened. Six strategic goals for the Serb people in Bosnia have been drafted: state separation, the Posavina corridor, the Drina valley border, the Una-Neretva border, the division of Sarajevo, and access to the sea. Your army commander has reviewed them. He warns the Assembly plainly: pursuing these goals — particularly the Drina corridor and Sarajevo — will require actions that constitute genocide. The Assembly awaits your decision.

effect.text: The strategic goals are presented to the Assembly.

response_options.label: Adopt all six goals
response_options.description: Full offensive doctrine. All axes active. The Drina valley will be cleared. Sarajevo will be divided. Your commander's warning is noted and disregarded.

future_consequences.label: Paramilitary policy decision opens
future_consequences.explanation: Adopting all six goals records rs_strategic_goals as all_six and makes the paramilitary-policy decision available — the historical RS leadership posture flows from this platform choice. The VOPP-rejection decision (May 1993) and the Belgrade embargo response (August 1994) are also reachable from this platform: the Six Strategic Goals foreclose Vance-Owen's ten-province scheme (Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T §§3471-3475) and lock the RS leadership onto the rejectionist line that triggers Belgrade's August 1994 embargo (Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T §§4263-4310; UNSCR 943). The same maximalist platform also locks RS posture toward NATO coercion in September 1995 (Deliberate Force compliance decision, Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T §§4940-4982) and the October 1995 Holbrooke-Belgrade channel posture decision (Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T §§4985-5020; Holbrooke ch. 8). The May 1995 UN hostage-crisis response decision is also reachable: maximum-tempo Sarajevo-axis fires draw NATO air strikes near Pale on 25-26 May 1995, and the VRS retaliation seizes 377 UN peacekeepers (Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T Count 11 §§5810-5876; Mladić IT-09-92-T Count 6 §§5169-5215; UNSCR 998).

future_consequences.label: UN hostage-crisis response decision (May 1995)
future_consequences.explanation: The all-six platform sustains the Sarajevo-axis siege fires and Drina-corridor operations that draw NATO air strikes near Pale on 25-26 May 1995. The VRS retaliation seizes 377 UN peacekeepers across more than 30 facilities (Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T Count 11 §§5810-5876; Mladić IT-09-92-T Count 6 §§5169-5215). The Pale leadership then faces the response-to-existing-state decision recorded by UNSCR 998 (16 June 1995) and UN S/1995/444 (30 May 1995). Per v1.3 packet §3.6 named-row carve-out, the decision is admissible because the hostages are already in state at fire-time; no response option authorizes new hostage-taking.

future_consequences.label: Vance-Owen rejection decision (May 1993)
future_consequences.explanation: The all-six platform is structurally incompatible with the Vance-Owen Peace Plan's ten-province ethnic mixing (Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T §§3471-3475; UN S/25221). The RS Assembly rejection at Bijeljina 5-6 May 1993 follows from this platform choice; Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T §§3526-3530 records the Pale leadership's acquiescence in the Assembly outcome. The same maximalist platform also produces the August 1994 rejection of the Contact Group plan that triggers Belgrade's embargo response (Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T §§4263-4310).

future_consequences.label: Owen-Stoltenberg response decision (Sep 1993)
future_consequences.explanation: The all-six platform reaches the September 1993 Owen-Stoltenberg Union of Three Republics response decision. The plan ratifies Republika Srpska as a constitutive ethnic republic with the Drina-valley axis preserved and Sarajevo division retained inside the tripartite frame; Belgrade's directive aligns Pale with acceptance (Owen, Balkan Odyssey Ch. 7; Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T Vol. III §§4263-4310). The maximalist platform structurally accepts the framework even as the corridor is narrowed — the diplomatic legitimization of Republika Srpska is the value capture; the historical default (accept) follows from this platform. The reject counterfactual carries a steep patron-pressure spike per Belgrade-blessed diplomacy on this branch.

future_consequences.label: Belgrade pressure response decision (autumn 1993)
future_consequences.explanation: The all-six platform reaches the autumn 1993 Belgrade soft-diplomatic-pressure response decision. Milosevic's envoys arrive at Pale through the documented FRY-RS channel to press for tempo restraint on the Drina-corridor axis and signalled flexibility on the Sarajevo allocation under the Owen-Stoltenberg envelope (ICTY Krajisnik IT-00-39-T §§1006-1040; Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T Vol. III §§4263-4310). The maximalist platform produces defiance (defy_belgrade_directive) as the documented historical posture: the Six Strategic Goals matter more than the patron channel until the August 1994 embargo forces re-evaluation. Counterfactuals (accept_belgrade_directive, partial_compliance, broker_compromise) remain structurally reachable but their cost floors scale with platform intensity — patron-confidence flip is real, but the internal-cohesion damage on the accept counterfactual is most severe on this branch as Pale hawks read directive compliance as platform betrayal (recruitment penalty 0.90x / 6 turns). The broker-compromise counterfactual via Patriarch Pavle and the Russian envoys captures the Holbrooke-era diplomatic optionality (negotiating_leverage +10). This row is DISTINCT from `all_six_to_belgrade_embargo` — autumn 1993 is the soft-pressure phase (no material rupture); August 1994 is the hard embargo phase (FRY border closure, supply rupture). Per Wave 2 Canon §3.6 forward-looking guard, no downstream csq_rs_belgrade_pressure_* cascade may re-author cleansing, forced-displacement, hostage-taking, civilian-targeting, paramilitary deployment, or any sensitive-act response option; the Belgrade-Pale pressure lane is constitutional-political crisis scope, NOT operational ethnic-targeting.

future_consequences.label: Independence vs autonomy posture decision (autumn 1993)
future_consequences.explanation: The all-six platform reaches the autumn 1993 general RS posture decision between independence trajectory and negotiated-autonomy fallback frameworks. Between the May 1993 VOPP rejection at Bijeljina (Karadzic IT-95-5/18-T §§3526-3530) and the August 1994 Contact Group 51/49 rejection (Karadzic IT-95-5/18-T §§4263-4310), Pale leadership crystallizes its GENERAL posture between independence trajectory vs negotiated-autonomy fallback envelope (Knin-style autonomous province, asymmetric federation entity status, or minority-rights-only constitutional package). The all-six platform produces pursue_independence as the over-determined historical posture: the Six Strategic Goals at maximum scope structurally repudiate any autonomy fallback envelope; Belgrade's signalled willingness to accept negotiated autonomy through the Patriarch Pavle channel and Milosevic's private envoys runs into the platform's territorial maximalism. Counterfactuals (negotiate_autonomy_within_bih, accept_federation_status, accept_minority_rights_only) remain structurally reachable but their cost floors peak on this branch — internal_cohesion damage scales with platform intensity, and Pale-hawk revolt is most severe on the maximum platform when the leadership concedes the maximalist claim. This row is DISTINCT from R1 (foundational Six Strategic Goals 1992 platform), R6 (specific VOPP plan response May 1993), R7 (soft Belgrade pressure 1993), R8 (hard Belgrade embargo August 1994) — R12 captures the GENERAL posture decision between specific plan-response windows. Per Wave 2 Canon §3.6 forward-looking guard, no downstream csq_rs_autonomy_* cascade may re-author cleansing, forced-displacement, civilian-targeting, hostage-taking, paramilitary deployment, ethnic-targeting, or any sensitive-act response option; the autonomy-path decision lane is constitutional-political crisis scope, NOT operational ethnic-targeting. The Drina-corridor cleansing, Sarajevo-siege fires, Srebrenica enclave operations, Prijedor camps exposure, and Drina valley campaign atrocity surfaces remain canon-gated through their existing event surfaces (drina_valley_ethnic_cleansing_1992, prijedor_camps_revealed_1992, srebrenica_falls_1995, un_hostage_crisis_1995, deliberate_force_rs_compliance_1995, drina_cleansing_decision_1992, concentration_camps_revealed_1992) and may not be re-opened or re-authored by any csq_rs_autonomy_* descendant.

future_consequences.label: Washington Agreement response decision (March 1994)
future_consequences.explanation: The all-six platform sets the structural conditions for the documented Pale non-engagement with the Washington Agreement (1 + 18 March 1994). The maximalist platform produces non-engagement (reject_federation) as the documented historical posture; trilateral counter-proposal, conditional engagement, and observer-status counterfactuals remain structurally reachable but their cost floors scale with platform intensity — patron-confidence collapse and internal cohesion damage peak on the observer-status counterfactual. Per Wave 2 Canon §3.6 forward-looking guard, no downstream csq_rs_washington_* cascade may re-author cleansing, paramilitary deployment, hostage-taking, or any new sensitive-history act; the Washington Agreement aftermath surfaces (Federation military integration, 1995 joint operations) remain canon-gated through their existing event surfaces.

future_consequences.label: Belgrade embargo decision (Aug 1994)
future_consequences.explanation: The all-six platform is incompatible with the Contact Group's 51/49 framework; the RS Assembly's July 1994 rejection of the Contact Group plan triggers the FRY embargo of 4 August 1994 (Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T §§4263-4310; UNSCR 943 of 23 September 1994). The Pale leadership then faces the patron-relations decision recorded by Karadžić §§4263-4310.

future_consequences.label: Contact Group 51/49 response decision (July 1994)
future_consequences.explanation: The all-six platform is structurally incompatible with the Contact Group 51/49 territorial framework presented by the US/UK/FR/DE/RU in early July 1994. The Pale Assembly's 3 August 1994 rejection (Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T §§4263-4310) is over-determined on this platform: the corridor, Drina-valley, and Sarajevo-division claims foreclose acceptance of the 51:49 map. The Pale leadership faces the historical reject vs counterfactual accept posture decision; the accept counterfactual carries a maximum cost floor (patron-pressure spike + internal-cohesion collapse + military-credibility loss) per platform intensity (UNSCR 942 / UNSCR 943 of 23 September 1994; Holbrooke To End a War Ch. 5).

future_consequences.label: Deliberate Force compliance decision (Sep 1995)
future_consequences.explanation: The all-six platform locks RS posture onto the Sarajevo-division and Drina-corridor axes whose military expression (Sarajevo siege fires, Markale II shelling) draws NATO Operation Deliberate Force (30 Aug-14 Sep 1995). Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T §§4940-4982 and Mladić IT-09-92-T §§4631-4685 record the September 1995 compliance decision; UN S/1995/755 authorizes the air campaign. The maximalist platform leaves the leadership facing the heavy-weapons withdrawal vs absorb-strikes posture choice.

future_consequences.label: Holbrooke US-Belgrade channel decision (Oct 1995)
future_consequences.explanation: The all-six platform leads Holbrooke to bypass Pale entirely and route US pressure through Milošević in Belgrade (Holbrooke, To End a War ch. 8). The Pale leadership faces the comply-with-Belgrade vs defy-US-framework posture decision; Milošević IT-02-54-T §§245-298 records the scope of the delegated authority. The maximalist platform raises the political cost of acquiescence but the post-Deliberate Force military exhaustion structurally binds the decision toward compliance.

future_consequences.label: Karadžić-Mladić split decision (Aug 1995)
future_consequences.explanation: The all-six platform sustains the Drina-corridor and Sarajevo-division operations whose late-July 1995 setbacks at Grahovo and Glamoč (HV/HVO Operation Summer '95, 25-29 July 1995) trigger Karadžić's 4 August 1995 decree purporting to dismiss Mladić from command of the VRS Main Staff. The maximalist platform binds the political leadership to a maximum-tempo war it then blames the general for failing to win, producing the seven-day command-paralysis crisis that Karadžić rescinds on 11 August 1995 (ICTY Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T §§5648-5703; ICTY Mladić IT-09-92-T §§4762-4778; UN A/54/549 §§270-280; BB II pp. 358-366). The Pale leadership then faces the back-down vs press-the-dismissal posture decision; the historical action was to rescind. Per Wave 2 Canon §3.6 forward-looking guard, neither option authorizes any new sensitive-history act — the dispute is Ring-2 internal RS command politics, and no downstream csq_vrs_command_paralysis cascade may re-author paramilitary deployment, cleansing, or hostage-taking.

future_consequences.label: Dayton acceptance decision (Nov 1995)
future_consequences.explanation: The all-six platform reaches the November 1995 Pale-side ratification of the General Framework Agreement initialed by Milošević at Dayton on 21 November 1995 (UN S/1995/999; UN S/RES/1031 of 15 December 1995). The maximalist platform raises the political cost of acquiescence — the Sarajevo-unification and eastern-enclave provisions are most painful to a Six-Goals platform — but the post-Deliberate Force military exhaustion and the Patriarch Paper delegation authority structurally bind the Pale leadership to the ratification decision (Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T §§5020-5067; Mladić IT-09-92-T §§4750-4795; ICJ Bosnia v. Serbia 26 Feb 2007).

Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T §§3526-3530 records the Bijeljina 5-6 May 1993 Assembly rejection; the maximum-tempo path compresses the runway to that decision but does not change its inevitability. The same platform also forecloses the 1994 Contact Group 51/49 framework and triggers Belgrade's 4 August 1994 embargo (Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T §§4263-4310).

future_consequences.label: Owen-Stoltenberg response decision (Sep 1993)
future_consequences.explanation: The maximum-force platform reaches the September 1993 Owen-Stoltenberg Union of Three Republics response decision. Even at maximum intensity, the documented Pale acceptance posture follows: the plan ratifies Republika Srpska as a constitutive ethnic republic with the Drina-valley axis preserved and Sarajevo division retained inside the tripartite frame; Belgrade's directive transmitted via Milosevic aligns Pale with acceptance (Owen, Balkan Odyssey Ch. 7; Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T Vol. III §§4263-4310). The diplomatic legitimization of Republika Srpska is over-determined on this branch. The reject counterfactual remains structurally reachable but its cost floor scales with the platform intensity — patron-pressure spike from Belgrade peaks on this path.

future_consequences.label: Belgrade pressure response decision (autumn 1993)
future_consequences.explanation: The maximum-force platform reaches the autumn 1993 Belgrade soft-diplomatic-pressure response decision a fortiori. Milosevic's envoys arrive at Pale through the documented FRY-RS channel to press for tempo restraint on the Drina-corridor axis and signalled flexibility on the Sarajevo allocation under the Owen-Stoltenberg envelope (ICTY Krajisnik IT-00-39-T §§1006-1040; Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T Vol. III §§4263-4310). Maximum-force intensity drives the documented defiance (defy_belgrade_directive) as over-determined: the Six Strategic Goals at maximum tempo cannot be reconciled with FRY tempo-restraint pressure, and the patron channel takes the friction. Counterfactuals (accept_belgrade_directive, partial_compliance, broker_compromise) remain structurally reachable but their cost floors peak — accept_belgrade_directive carries the most severe internal-cohesion damage on this branch (Pale hawks read directive compliance as platform repudiation at maximum tempo) and the six-turn recruitment penalty (0.90x pool) reflects the maximum platform-faction backlash. Broker-compromise via Patriarch Pavle and the Russian envoys preserves the negotiating-leverage gain but the optical patron-channel friction remains material. This row is DISTINCT from `aggressive_to_belgrade_embargo` — autumn 1993 is the soft-pressure phase (no material rupture); August 1994 is the hard embargo phase (FRY border closure, supply rupture). Per Wave 2 Canon §3.6 forward-looking guard, no downstream csq_rs_belgrade_pressure_* cascade may re-author cleansing, forced-displacement, hostage-taking, civilian-targeting, paramilitary deployment, or any sensitive-act response option; the Belgrade-Pale pressure lane is constitutional-political crisis scope, NOT operational ethnic-targeting.

future_consequences.label: Independence vs autonomy posture decision (autumn 1993)
future_consequences.explanation: The maximum-force platform reaches the autumn 1993 general RS posture decision between independence trajectory and negotiated-autonomy fallback frameworks a fortiori. Between the May 1993 VOPP rejection at Bijeljina (Karadzic IT-95-5/18-T §§3526-3530) and the August 1994 Contact Group 51/49 rejection (Karadzic IT-95-5/18-T §§4263-4310), Pale leadership crystallizes its GENERAL posture between independence trajectory vs negotiated-autonomy fallback envelope (Knin-style autonomous province, asymmetric federation entity status, or minority-rights-only constitutional package). The maximum-force platform produces pursue_independence as the over-determined historical posture: the Six Strategic Goals at maximum intensity structurally foreclose any autonomy fallback envelope, even as Belgrade's signalled willingness to accept negotiated autonomy through the Patriarch Pavle channel offers material relief from the FRY sanctions regime. Counterfactuals (negotiate_autonomy_within_bih, accept_federation_status, accept_minority_rights_only) remain structurally reachable but their cost floors peak on this branch — internal_cohesion damage scales with maximum platform intensity, Pale-hawk revolt is most severe on the maximum platform when the leadership concedes the maximalist claim, and the recruitment penalty under accept_minority_rights_only (0.85x pool / 10 turns) reflects the maximum platform-faction backlash. This row is DISTINCT from R1 (foundational Six Strategic Goals 1992 platform), R6 (specific VOPP plan response May 1993), R7 (soft Belgrade pressure 1993), R8 (hard Belgrade embargo August 1994) — R12 captures the GENERAL posture decision between specific plan-response windows. Per Wave 2 Canon §3.6 forward-looking guard, no downstream csq_rs_autonomy_* cascade may re-author cleansing, forced-displacement, civilian-targeting, hostage-taking, paramilitary deployment, ethnic-targeting, or any sensitive-act response option; the autonomy-path decision lane is constitutional-political crisis scope, NOT operational ethnic-targeting. The Drina-corridor cleansing, Sarajevo-siege fires, Srebrenica enclave operations, Prijedor camps exposure, and Drina valley campaign atrocity surfaces remain canon-gated through their existing event surfaces (drina_valley_ethnic_cleansing_1992, prijedor_camps_revealed_1992, srebrenica_falls_1995, un_hostage_crisis_1995, deliberate_force_rs_compliance_1995, drina_cleansing_decision_1992, concentration_camps_revealed_1992) and may not be re-opened or re-authored by any csq_rs_autonomy_* descendant.

future_consequences.label: Washington Agreement response decision (March 1994)
future_consequences.explanation: The maximum-force platform produces the documented Pale non-engagement with the Washington Agreement (1 + 18 March 1994) a fortiori. The bipolar Federation framework is structurally incompatible with the Six Strategic Goals at maximum intensity — the corridor, the Drina-valley axis, and Sarajevo division are all foreclosed by the Federation constitutional architecture (Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T §§3526-3530; Holbrooke, To End a War, Ch. 4-5). Non-engagement (reject_federation) is over-determined on this platform; the trilateral counter-proposal, conditional engagement, and observer-status counterfactuals remain structurally reachable but their cost floors peak — patron-confidence collapse and internal cohesion damage on the observer-status counterfactual hit their maximum on the maximum-force platform, where Pale hawks read observer status as capitulation to a framework Karadzic has publicly disdained. Per Wave 2 Canon §3.6 forward-looking guard, no downstream csq_rs_washington_* cascade may re-author cleansing, paramilitary deployment, hostage-taking, or any new sensitive-history act; the Washington Agreement aftermath surfaces (Federation military integration, 1995 joint operations) remain canon-gated through their existing event surfaces.

future_consequences.label: Belgrade embargo decision (Aug 1994)
future_consequences.explanation: The maximum-force platform is structurally incompatible with the Contact Group 51/49 territorial framework. The RS Assembly's July 1994 rejection of the Contact Group plan is a direct consequence of this platform, triggering Belgrade's 4 August 1994 embargo and the Pale leadership's patron-relations decision (Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T §§4263-4310; UNSCR 943 of 23 September 1994).

future_consequences.label: Contact Group 51/49 response decision (July 1994)
future_consequences.explanation: The maximum-force platform forecloses the Contact Group 51:49 framework a fortiori: the Six Goals at maximum intensity are structurally incompatible with the proposed map. The Pale Assembly's 3 August 1994 rejection (Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T §§4263-4310) is over-determined on this branch, and the counterfactual accept posture remains structurally available but its cost floor scales with platform intensity — patron-pressure spike, internal-cohesion collapse, military-credibility damage, and recruitment-pool penalty all peak on this path (UNSCR 942 / UNSCR 943 of 23 September 1994; Holbrooke To End a War Ch. 5).

future_consequences.label: Deliberate Force compliance decision (Sep 1995)
future_consequences.explanation: The maximum-force platform drives Sarajevo siege fires and the Markale II shelling pattern at maximum intensity, accelerating the path to NATO Operation Deliberate Force (30 Aug-14 Sep 1995, UN S/1995/755). Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T §§4940-4982 and Mladić IT-09-92-T §§4631-4685 record the September 1995 leadership decision; Holbrooke, To End a War, ch. 8 corroborates. The Pale leadership faces the heavy-weapons withdrawal vs absorb-strikes posture choice under the heaviest NATO pressure of the war.

future_consequences.label: Holbrooke US-Belgrade channel decision (Oct 1995)
future_consequences.explanation: The maximum-force platform makes the October 1995 Holbrooke-Belgrade channel decision a fortiori: Milošević's willingness to negotiate the substantive Dayton framework under the Patriarch Paper delegation (Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T §§4985-5020; Holbrooke ch. 8) is precisely what allows the US to bypass a Pale leadership that has discredited itself with the maximum-intensity Sarajevo-axis fires. The Pale leadership faces the comply-with-Belgrade vs defy-US-framework decision under maximum pressure (Geneva framework UN S/1995/780; New York principles UN S/1995/827; Milošević IT-02-54-T §§245-298). The defy counterfactual remains structurally reachable but its cost floor scales with the platform intensity — patron-confidence collapse, FRY supply pinch, and Belgrade-imposed leadership change risk all peak on this path.

future_consequences.label: Karadžić-Mladić split decision (Aug 1995)
future_consequences.explanation: The maximum-force platform drives the Drina-corridor and Sarajevo-division axes at maximum intensity, accelerating the late-July 1995 reverses at Grahovo and Glamoč (HV/HVO Operation Summer '95, 25-29 July 1995) that provide the operational pretext for Karadžić's 4 August 1995 decree dismissing Mladić from command of the VRS Main Staff. The platform binds the political leadership to a maximum-tempo war it then blames the general for failing to win; the officer revolt (eighteen senior officers including all five corps commanders) and seven-day command-paralysis crisis follow a fortiori, and Karadžić rescinds on 11 August 1995 (ICTY Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T §§5648-5703; ICTY Mladić IT-09-92-T §§4762-4778; UN A/54/549 §§270-280; BB II pp. 358-366). The Pale leadership faces the back-down vs press-the-dismissal posture decision; the historical action was to rescind. The press-the-dismissal counterfactual remains structurally available but its cost floor scales with the platform intensity — internal cohesion collapse and military credibility damage peak on this path. Per Wave 2 Canon §3.6 forward-looking guard, neither option authorizes any new sensitive-history act.

future_consequences.label: Dayton acceptance decision (Nov 1995)
future_consequences.explanation: Even the maximum-force platform reaches the November 1995 Pale-side ratification of the General Framework Agreement initialed by Milošević at Dayton on 21 November 1995 (UN S/1995/999; UN S/RES/1031 of 15 December 1995). The Sarajevo-unification and eastern-enclave provisions are most painful to a maximum-tempo platform but the post-Deliberate Force military exhaustion, the Patriarch Paper delegation authority, and the Federation ground offensive halted only by the Holbrooke 51:49 line bind the RS National Assembly's ratification vote (Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T §§5020-5067; Mladić IT-09-92-T §§4750-4795; ICJ Bosnia v. Serbia 26 Feb 2007). The hardline counterfactual remains structurally available but its cost floor scales with the platform intensity.

RBiH.headline: RS Assembly endorses Six Strategic Goals
RBiH.body: Belgrade-aligned deputies adopt Karadzic's territorial maximalist platform. Sarajevo intelligence reads this as a hardening of war aims; federal options narrow.

HRHB.headline: Karadzic Assembly clarifies territorial reach
HRHB.body: RS adoption of the Six Goals sharpens corridor and ethnic-separation claims that bear on western Herzegovina; Mostar leadership weighs patron consultation.

RBiH.headline: Pale narrows its strategic platform
RBiH.body: RS leaders signal a selective war-aim line centered on corridor security and restraint around the Drina valley and Sarajevo. Sarajevo reads the move as less openly maximalist, but still partition-minded.

HRHB.headline: RS Assembly adopts selective goals
HRHB.body: Pale emphasizes corridor security while tempering some territorial objectives. Mostar sees a platform that may reduce immediate escalation but keeps western and central claims unsettled.

RBiH.headline: RS signals maximum-force doctrine
RBiH.body: Pale adopts the Six Goals at maximum intensity despite its command warning. Sarajevo reads the decision as a severe escalation in RS war aims and international-risk exposure.

HRHB.headline: Pale hardens territorial doctrine
HRHB.body: RS leaders choose maximum force behind the full strategic platform. Mostar assesses a more dangerous RS posture, with corridor and separation claims likely to shape every front.

historical_source: ICTY Karadzic Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T, 24 March 2016) paras. 2710-2715, 3447-3526 — Six Strategic Goals and JCE findings. ICTY Mladic Trial Judgment (IT-09-92-T, 22 November 2017) paras. 3232-3243 — commander's Assembly warning. ICJ Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro (26 February 2007).

title: Paramilitary Authorization Policy
narrative: The Ministry of Interior has drafted a deployment protocol for the volunteer formations operating alongside the regular army. Arkan's Tigers, the White Eagles, the Yellow Wasps, the Red Berets — names known to the Crisis Staffs in Banja Luka and Prijedor, names that travel ahead of the columns into the villages. The pattern is documented: rear-area pocket cleanup, civilian columns moved off the land, detention sites established in the wake. The political files require a posture. Authorize on standing orders, review each deployment, or refuse the formations entry to the order of battle.

effect.text: The Presidency records a paramilitary deployment policy.

source_note: ICTY Karadzic, Stakic, Brdjanin, Tadic, Krajisnik, and Šešelj findings document the political leadership's tolerance of paramilitary methods. UN reports record the pattern contemporaneously. The historical RS posture was de-facto tolerance.
staff_assessment: Standing authorization mirrors documented RS leadership posture. Per-deployment review introduces command friction; refusal forecloses paramilitary operations entirely and shifts the rear-area burden onto regular formations.
trigger_evidence: The Six Strategic Goals platform has been recorded; rear-area operations follow.
Crisis Staffs in Banja Luka and Prijedor are already coordinating with volunteer formations.

response_options.label: Always allow paramilitary deployment
response_options.description: Standing authorization. Arkan, the White Eagles, the Yellow Wasps, and the MUP Special Police deploy on local request without per-mission review. Each approved sweep records civilian casualties and increments the war-crimes counter; the international monitors will see the pattern.

future_consequences.label: Paramilitary sweep engine is the canon-bound consequence surface
future_consequences.explanation: Standing authorization routes paramilitary capture through the existing paramilitary_sweep engine; civilian casualties and war_crimes_events are recorded automatically — not by this option's effects.

response_options.label: Ask per deployment
response_options.description: Each proposed sweep arrives in the Presidency files with a casualty projection. The Crisis Staffs lose blanket authority; the political center retains the decision. Operational tempo slows; the international monitors note the reviews.

future_consequences.label: Per-deployment modal becomes the player surface
future_consequences.explanation: Per-decision review routes each proposed sweep through a modal with full casualty projection. The csq_paramilitary_authorization_refused counterfactual remains reachable if approvals are never granted.

response_options.label: Always deny paramilitary deployment
response_options.description: The volunteer formations are refused entry to the order of battle. Rear-area operations fall to regular VRS units and MUP regulars. The hardline base is alienated; the international monitors note the absence of the pattern they expect to find.

future_consequences.label: Counterfactual paramilitary refusal consequence opens
future_consequences.explanation: Refusing paramilitary deployment forecloses paramilitary sweeps on the RS side and opens the counterfactual refusal consequence; bot factions continue historical paramilitary use per the canonical engine surface.

RBiH.headline: RS Presidency authorizes paramilitary standing orders
RBiH.body: Pale records standing authorization for Arkan-style formations to operate alongside regular VRS units. Sarajevo reads the policy as a continuation of the rear-area pattern documented since Bijeljina.

HRHB.headline: Pale formalizes paramilitary tolerance
HRHB.body: RS leaders confirm volunteer formations remain on local-request authority. Mostar staff note the policy hardens the rear-area pattern across the Krajina and Drina.

RBiH.headline: RS shifts to per-deployment paramilitary review
RBiH.body: Pale signals a reviewable posture for volunteer formations; Sarajevo reads the change as posture signaling rather than a settled disengagement.

HRHB.headline: RS introduces paramilitary review process
HRHB.body: Pale routes each volunteer deployment through political review; Mostar staff assess slower rear-area tempo without a clear break in the pattern.

RBiH.headline: RS refuses paramilitary deployment
RBiH.body: Pale records a refusal of volunteer formations on the order of battle. Sarajevo reads the choice as a counter-historical posture; the rear-area pattern would not match the documented record.

HRHB.headline: RS denies paramilitary formations entry
HRHB.body: Pale shuts the volunteer formations out of the order of battle. Mostar staff note the absence of the documented rear-area pattern; regular VRS units carry the load.

historical_source: ICTY Karadzic Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T, 24 March 2016) paras. 2470-2509, 3469-3475, 3505-3524. ICTY Stakic Trial Judgment (IT-97-24-T, 31 July 2003) paras. 88-98, 490-518. ICTY Brdjanin Trial Judgment (IT-99-36-T, 1 September 2004) paras. 108-123, 1051-1149. ICTY Tadic Trial Judgment (IT-94-1-T, 7 May 1997). ICTY Krajisnik Trial Judgment (IT-00-39-T, 27 September 2006) paras. 856-891. ICTY Šešelj Appeal Judgment (IT-03-67-A, 11 April 2018). UN A/54/549 para. 35. UN S/1994/674 (Commission of Experts Final Report, Annex III.A — Special Forces).

title: What Is Bosnia?
narrative: Your Presidency must declare its vision for the state. The platform drafted in May declares a multi-ethnic, civic republic where all citizens are equal regardless of ethnicity. But the war is testing that ideal. Serb and Croat soldiers serve in your army — for now. Some in your party argue that this is a Bosniak struggle, not a civic one. The international community watches closely. Your declaration will shape who fights for you, who supports you, and what you are fighting for.
source_note: Karadzic judgment context on Bosnia's statehood dispute; ARBiH composition and Divjak are cited for wartime multi-ethnic service.
staff_assessment: The Sarajevo Presidency preserves its civic claim and international posture by keeping the republic defined around equal citizenship, while accepting friction with harder wartime national currents.
trigger_evidence: The May 1992 platform debate is before the Presidency.
Wartime mobilization is forcing Sarajevo to state the political basis of the republic it claims to defend.

response_options.label: Civic multi-ethnic republic
response_options.description: One republic, all citizens equal. Serbs and Croats serve alongside Bosniaks. The world respects this. Your nationalists resent it.

future_consequences.label: Civic platform follow-through
future_consequences.explanation: Choosing the civic platform records rbih_state_identity as civic, opening the paramilitary-policy decision, the Vance-Owen acceptance branch, the Owen-Stoltenberg Assembly-rejection branch, the Srebrenica demilitarization decision (April-May 1993), the Abdic / APWB rupture posture decision (27 September 1993), the Washington Agreement acceptance branch, the NATO ultimatum HWEZ compliance decision (February 1994), the Federation Army integration depth decision (mid-1994), the Bihac 5th Corps offensive decision (autumn 1994), the late-war territorial-reintegration offensive decision (Aug-Sept 1995), and the Dayton acceptance branch (Nov 1995), and making the civic consolidation branch visible if its later conditions are met.

future_consequences.label: RBiH minority officer/recruitment retention decision (Aug 1992)
future_consequences.explanation: The civic platform structurally aligns Sarajevo's posture with the documented multi-ethnic ARBiH composition decision: retention of Gen. Jovan Divjak (Serb) at the Sarajevo HQ Deputy Commander post from April 1992, Stjepan Šiber (Croat) on the General Staff, and the mixed-ethnicity 1st Corps Sarajevo defense units throughout the war. The civic line reads ethnic vetting and purges as institutionally suicidal — the civic platform's commitment to equal citizenship requires multi-ethnic officer retention as a structural foundation of state legitimacy. The documented historical posture is retain_minorities; the gradual_purge and mandatory_purge counterfactuals collapse the civic claim at the institutional level (cohesion/legitimacy/recruitment costs); the federated_units counterfactual is the intermediate compromise (Balkan Battlegrounds Vol. II ARBiH composition + General Staff; Jovan Divjak, 'Sarajevo, Mon Amour' Buchet/Chastel 2004 ch. on Sarajevo HQ Deputy Commander posting; Marko Attila Hoare, 'How Bosnia Armed' Saqi 2004 on civic-republic posture preserving minority service; ICTY Galić IT-98-29-T + Dragomir Milošević IT-98-29/1-T + Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T Vol. III on ARBiH 1st Corps command structure).

future_consequences.label: Washington Agreement acceptance path (March 1994)
future_consequences.explanation: The civic platform aligns Sarajevo's posture with the multi-ethnic Federation framework: U.S. shuttle diplomacy (Christopher, Galbraith, Redman) plus the Markale-context pressure makes the March 1994 Washington Agreement decision reachable once turn ~102 arrives. Civic identity strengthens the diplomatic case for acceptance (Washington Agreement text 1 + 18 March 1994; Vienna Framework 26 March 1994; Bosnian Presidency Athens-channel records; BB Vol. II pp. 451-455).

future_consequences.label: Federation Army integration depth decision (mid-1994)
future_consequences.explanation: The civic platform reaches the mid-1994 Federation Army (HVOBiH / VFBiH) integration depth decision. The Washington Agreement of 1 + 18 March 1994 established the Federation Army on paper; the institutional reality lagged, with persistent ARBiH-HVO parallel command structures documented in ICRC field reports across Mostar, Vitez, Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, Konjic, and Jablanica. The civic platform's commitment to a unified multi-ethnic republic structurally aligns Sarajevo's posture with the Federation Army architecture, while the documented historical posture remains acceptance of parallel commands per BB Vol. II pp. 451-455 + Ch. 12 (Federation Army institutional friction persistence through Vienna, Contact Group, and Dayton). The full_integration counterfactual amplifies the civic-Federation institutional consolidation; the refuse_integration counterfactual ruptures the Washington framework with a US patron-pressure spike (Washington Agreement text 1 + 18 March 1994; Vienna Framework 26 March 1994; Prlic IT-04-74-T Vol. 1 §§452-470, Vol. 3 §§120-200; US embassy archived reporting).

future_consequences.label: Srebrenica demilitarization decision (April-May 1993)
future_consequences.explanation: The civic platform reaches the April-May 1993 Srebrenica demilitarization decision: under UN Security Council Resolution 819 (16 April 1993) and the Sarajevo-airport agreement of 18 April 1993 (extended at Žepa on 8 May 1993), the Presidency must declare a compliance posture toward the UNPROFOR-supervised weapons handover inside the enclave. The civic line carries no special inclination to defy a UN-brokered humanitarian framework; the documented historical posture remains partial/nominal compliance per the UN Secretary-General's report on the fall of Srebrenica (UN A/54/549 of 15 November 1999, §§57-98) and the ICTY Krstić Trial Judgement (IT-98-33-T, 2 August 2001, §§16-28).

future_consequences.label: Owen-Stoltenberg Assembly-rejection path (September 1993)
future_consequences.explanation: The civic platform's commitment to a unified multi-ethnic republic structurally aligns Sarajevo's posture with the documented Assembly-led rejection of the Owen-Stoltenberg partition framework: the Presidency's narrow Invincible acceptance of 20 September 1993 is overturned by the Sarajevo Assembly session of 29 September 1993, citing the unrecoverable Drina enclaves and Posavina corridor (UN S/26486; UN S/26922; ICTY Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T vol. III §§4263-4310).

future_consequences.label: Arms-embargo lift-and-strike advocacy decision (September 1993)
future_consequences.explanation: The civic platform structurally aligns Sarajevo's posture with the documented lift-and-strike diplomatic offensive of 1993-1995: the moral-high-ground appeal of the asymmetric-application argument (UNSCR 713 freezes the pre-war JNA force distribution privileging the VRS and HVO over the under-armed ARBiH) is most coherent on the civic line because the legitimate-grievance external-advocacy framework rests on the civic-republic identity claim — Izetbegović's UN General Assembly addresses + Silajdžić's Washington-London-Bonn shuttle diplomacy + the US Senate S.J. Res. 110 of 11 August 1993 and the Dole-Lieberman amendment of July-August 1995 (vetoed by Clinton both times) all operated through the civic-republic legitimacy frame at the moral-high-ground end. The civic line carries no special inclination toward the seek_clandestine_arms counterfactual (the Iran channel + Mujahideen-brigade recruitment is in tension with the civic-republic external posture); the abandon_lift_advocacy counterfactual is institutionally inconsistent with the civic platform's external-advocacy commitment; the accept_embargo counterfactual collapses the asymmetric-application argument and is hardest on the civic line precisely because it forecloses the diplomatic-leverage framework that the civic posture has been building (UNSCR 713 of 25 September 1991; Balkan Battlegrounds Vol. II — 1993-95 ARBiH supply chronology + Silajdžić diplomatic posture; Alija Izetbegović 'Inescapable Questions' Islamic Foundation 2003 — UN General Assembly addresses; Richard Holbrooke 'To End A War' Random House 1998 chs. 4-6; US Senate Foreign Relations Committee records on S.J. Res. 110 + Dole-Lieberman amendment; UN A/54/549 §§ on UNSCR 713 application + lift-and-strike diplomacy; ICTY Halilović IT-01-48-T on ARBiH General Staff supply situation 1993). §3.6 STRICT — Iran/Mujahideen sensitive territory remains canon-gated through existing event surfaces (paramilitary-policy, rbih_paramilitary_policy_1992); no atrocity-coupled choices reachable from any csq_rbih_embargo_* descendant.

future_consequences.label: Abdic / APWB rupture posture decision (27 September 1993)
future_consequences.explanation: The civic platform reaches the Abdic / APWB rupture posture decision of 27 September 1993. Fikret Abdic's declaration of the Autonomous Province of Western Bosnia at Velika Kladusa opens an internal front inside the Bihac pocket against the civic platform's commitment to a unified multi-ethnic republic. The civic line structurally aligns Sarajevo with non-recognition of APWB and 5th Corps clearance operations as capacity allows, cascading through Operation Tigar (March 1994), the August 1994 Velika Kladusa clearance, the RS/RSK/APWB Pauk counter-offensive (autumn 1994), and the post-Storm final clearance window (August 1995). The Bihac 5th Corps offensive decision (autumn 1994) carries forward the operational lane (Balkan Battlegrounds Vol. II Bihac-pocket chronology; UNSCR 824/836/900 Bihac safe-area regime; UN S/1994/674 Annex VI and VII; Karlovac County Court verdict 31 July 2002 on Abdic).

future_consequences.label: NATO ultimatum HWEZ compliance decision (February 1994)
future_consequences.explanation: The civic platform aligns Sarajevo's posture with the NATO-led Sarajevo Heavy Weapons Exclusion Zone regime imposed by the North Atlantic Council ultimatum of 9 February 1994 following the Markale market shelling of 5 February 1994 (68 civilians killed; ICTY Galić IT-98-29-T attributing attribution to SRK/VRS positions). The civic line carries Sarajevo's documented cooperation with UNPROFOR HWEZ inspections and public framing of NATO enforcement as overdue Western action: the Presidency accepts the symmetric application of withdrawal demands to ARBiH heavy weapons inside the 20km perimeter (NATO NAC decision 9 February 1994; UNSCR 836 of 4 June 1993; UN A/54/549 §§ on Sarajevo HWEZ regime; BB Vol. II Sarajevo siege chronology).

future_consequences.label: Bihac 5th Corps offensive decision (autumn 1994)
future_consequences.explanation: The civic platform reaches the autumn-1994 Bihac 5th Corps posture decision. Dudakovic's offensive plan against APWB (Velika Kladusa) and the VRS (Grabez, Bosanska Krupa) is the principal armed expression of the Sarajevo line against the Fikret Abdic split declared at Velika Kladusa on 27 September 1993. The civic platform's commitment to a unified multi-ethnic republic structurally aligns Sarajevo with pressing the offensive that liquidates (briefly) the APWB rear threat and catalyzes the international engagement decision tree leading to Operation Storm 1995 and Mistral/Sana 1995 (BB Vol. II pp. 406-417 region; UNSCR 958 of 19 November 1994; NATO 21 November 1994 Udbina close-air-support action).

future_consequences.label: Contact Group 51/49 response decision (July 1994)
future_consequences.explanation: The civic platform aligns Sarajevo's posture with the Contact Group 51:49 framework presented by the US/UK/FR/DE/RU in early July 1994: a multi-ethnic civic republic supports the Federation/RS dual-entity territorial settlement that anchors international recognition through Washington-track diplomacy. The Sarajevo Presidency faces the historical accept (under US/Contact-Group pressure, with reservations on the eastern enclaves) vs counterfactual reject posture decision; the reject counterfactual carries an international-standing penalty and a patron-pressure spike from defying explicit US pressure (Contact Group proposal, July 1994; Holbrooke To End a War Ch. 5; UNSCR 942 of 23 September 1994; Karadžić IT-95-5/18-T §§4263-4310 Pale Assembly contrast).

future_consequences.label: Dayton acceptance decision (November-December 1995)
future_consequences.explanation: The civic platform aligns Sarajevo's posture with the Federation/RS dual-entity arrangement inside a unitary multi-ethnic BiH preserved by the Dayton General Framework Agreement initialed 21 November 1995 and signed in Paris 14 December 1995 (UN S/1995/999; UN S/RES/1031 of 15 December 1995). Annex 4 (BiH Constitution) preserves RBiH legal continuity; Annex 7 (refugees and displaced persons) is the partial compensation for the Inter-Entity Boundary Line ratification of the eastern-enclave losses. The post-Srebrenica strategic conditions (Krstić IT-98-33-T 2 Aug 2001; ICJ Bosnia v. Serbia 26 Feb 2007) and the Contact Group 51:49 framework structurally bind the Presidency's acceptance under duress.

future_consequences.label: Late-war territorial-reintegration offensive decision (Aug-Sept 1995)
future_consequences.explanation: The civic platform reaches the August-September 1995 late-war territorial-reintegration offensive decision after the July Srebrenica/Žepa rupture, the 4 August Operation Storm Krajina liberation, the 30 August-14 September NATO Operation Deliberate Force, and the joint HV-HVO Operation Mistral 2. The civic-republic platform's commitment to a unitary multi-ethnic BiH structurally aligns Sarajevo with launch_coordinated_offensives as the documented historical posture: ARBiH 5th Corps Operation Sana (Bosanski Petrovac / Ključ / Sanski Most) breaking out of Bihać, ARBiH 3rd/7th Corps central-Bosnia flank operations paired with HV-HVO Mistral 2, recovering approximately 20% of pre-war RS-held territory and forcing Holbrooke's Geneva-New York framework to the 51:49 Dayton territorial floor (BB Vol. II Ch. 15-16; Holbrooke To End a War chs. 8-11; Izetbegović Inescapable Questions on the September offensive decision frame). The defensive_consolidation and wait_for_diplomacy counterfactuals collapse the Federation alliance and territorial-legitimacy capture; the accept_partition counterfactual ruptures the civic-republic unitary BiH claim at the constitutional level (territorial_legitimacy -40, military_credibility -30, internal_cohesion -25, international_standing -15 on the maximum counterfactual). §3.6 STRICT — the Operation Sana liberation of western Bosnia included some Serb-civilian displacement (ICTY Halilović IT-01-48-T context on ARBiH General Staff doctrine; UNHCR Sept-Oct 1995 reporting; HRW September-October 1995 western-Bosnia humanitarian fallout; HV-HVO Krajina civilian-column attribution canon-gated through hv_hvo_cooperation_1995 §3.6 source_note + Gotovina IT-06-90-T appeals JCE reversal context) — this decision is operational-strategic and no downstream csq_rbih_late_war_* cascade may re-author cleansing, forced-displacement, civilian-targeting, hostage-taking, paramilitary-deployment, or any sensitive-act response option.

The offer_federation_status counterfactual extends the HRHB channel symmetrically toward RS with a Bosniak-hawks internal_cohesion cost; the conditional_autonomy_proposal counterfactual threads the needle (RBiH sovereignty as the precondition); the accept_de_facto_partition counterfactual collapses the civic-republic claim at the constitutional level (territorial_legitimacy -40, military_credibility -25, internal_cohesion -25, international_standing -10). §3.6 STRICT — this decision is constitutional/diplomatic and no downstream csq_rbih_reintegration_* cascade may re-author cleansing, forced-displacement, civilian-targeting, hostage-taking, paramilitary-deployment, or any sensitive-act response option; the sensitive humanitarian surfaces of the war remain canon-gated through their existing event surfaces.

response_options.label: Bosniak national state
response_options.description: This is our land and our fight. Those who stand against us are not our citizens. Clear identity, clear purpose — but you lose minority soldiers and international sympathy.

future_consequences.explanation: Choosing the Bosniak national line records rbih_state_identity as bosniak_national, opening the paramilitary-policy decision, the Vance-Owen acceptance branch, the Owen-Stoltenberg Assembly-rejection branch, the Srebrenica demilitarization decision (April-May 1993), the Abdic / APWB rupture posture decision (27 September 1993), the Washington Agreement acceptance branch, the NATO ultimatum HWEZ compliance decision (February 1994), the Federation Army integration depth decision (mid-1994), the late-war territorial-reintegration offensive decision (Aug-Sept 1995), and the Dayton acceptance branch (Nov 1995), and making the minority-defection, unity, and diplomatic-disillusionment branches visible if their later conditions are met.

future_consequences.label: RBiH minority officer/recruitment retention decision (Aug 1992)
future_consequences.explanation: The Bosniak-national line reaches the August 1992 minority-retention posture decision with the gradual_purge and mandatory_purge counterfactuals over-determined at the SDA-nationalist faction level: the Bosniak-national platform amplifies the institutional pressure for ethnic vetting and dismissal of Serb and Croat officers from the ARBiH command. The documented historical posture remains retain_minorities — Izetbegović and the General Staff resisted internal Bosniak-nationalist pressure for purges across the war — but on this branch the institutional pressure to purge is loudest, the cohesion + recruitment + international-standing penalties of the purge counterfactuals are pulled forward, and the federated_units counterfactual reads as the closest Bosniak-national line variant (single-ethnicity unit structures under unified command preserve the platform's institutional preferences without the diplomatic rupture of mandatory_purge). The civic platform's structural foundation in multi-ethnic officer retention is weakened on this branch even when retain_minorities is the chosen response (Balkan Battlegrounds Vol. II ARBiH composition + General Staff; Jovan Divjak, 'Sarajevo, Mon Amour' Buchet/Chastel 2004; Marko Attila Hoare, 'How Bosnia Armed' Saqi 2004 on SDA-nationalist internal pressure).

future_consequences.label: Washington Agreement acceptance path (March 1994)
future_consequences.explanation: Even the Bosniak-national line is structurally bound to face the March 1994 Washington Agreement decision: U.S. shuttle diplomacy and the post-Markale NATO ultimatum push Sarajevo's Presidency into the Federation framework regardless of its 1992 identity declaration. Silajdzic-led skepticism is louder on this branch, but the framework still arrives (Washington Agreement text 1 + 18 March 1994; Vienna Framework 26 March 1994; BB Vol. II pp. 451-455).

future_consequences.label: Federation Army integration depth decision (mid-1994)
future_consequences.explanation: The Bosniak-national line reaches the mid-1994 Federation Army (HVOBiH / VFBiH) integration depth decision with the parallel-commands posture over-determined: a Bosniak-national platform amplifies the institutional preference for ARBiH operational independence inside the Federation framework. The Washington Agreement of 1 + 18 March 1994 established the Federation Army on paper, but BB Vol. II pp. 451-455 + Ch. 12 document the institutional friction persistence through Vienna, the Contact Group framework, and Dayton — Bosniak-national platform amplifies the friction. The full_integration counterfactual is most resented on this branch (Assembly nationalist faction reads it as ARBiH dilution); the refuse_integration counterfactual is loudest on this branch but ruptures the Washington framework with a US patron-pressure spike (Washington Agreement text 1 + 18 March 1994; Vienna Framework 26 March 1994; Prlic IT-04-74-T Vol. 1 §§452-470, Vol. 3 §§120-200; US embassy archived reporting).

future_consequences.label: Srebrenica demilitarization decision (April-May 1993)
future_consequences.explanation: The Bosniak-national line still reaches the April-May 1993 Srebrenica demilitarization decision under UN Security Council Resolution 819 (16 April 1993) and the UN-brokered Sarajevo-airport agreement of 18 April 1993 (extended at Žepa 8 May 1993). On this branch the 28th Division's combat-effective small-arms retention reads as a stronger institutional posture than on the civic line, but the documented historical posture remains partial/nominal compliance with UNPROFOR weapons-handover terms per UN A/54/549 (15 November 1999, §§57-98) and the ICTY Krstić Trial Judgement (IT-98-33-T, 2 August 2001, §§16-28).

future_consequences.explanation: The Bosniak-national line still reaches the Owen-Stoltenberg decision aboard HMS Invincible (20 September 1993). The defensive_consolidation counterfactual collapses the dual-track logic on the military axis (Federation alliance fray + thinner Dayton ground); the wait_for_diplomacy counterfactual is instrumentally inconsistent with the dual-track posture's reliance on visible military weight as Holbrooke-channel leverage; the accept_partition counterfactual is the maximum-cost rule-following discipline incompatible with both the external (civic-republic unitary BiH claim) and the inward (Bosniak institutional preservation) lanes — the cost floor stays PUNITIVE on this counterfactual (military_credibility -30, territorial_legitimacy -40, internal_cohesion -25, international_standing -15, alliance_change -0.15) even when the pragmatic instrumentalism reads concession as institutionally tempting (BB Vol. II Ch. 15-16; Holbrooke To End a War chs. 8-11; Izetbegović Inescapable Questions; ICTY Halilović IT-01-48-T on ARBiH General Staff late-war doctrine). §3.6 STRICT — the Operation Sana liberation of western Bosnia included some Serb-civilian displacement (ICTY Halilović IT-01-48-T context; UNHCR Sept-Oct 1995 reporting; HRW September-October 1995 western-Bosnia humanitarian fallout; HV-HVO Krajina civilian-column attribution canon-gated through hv_hvo_cooperation_1995 §3.6 source_note + Gotovina IT-06-90-T appeals JCE reversal context) — this decision is operational-strategic and no downstream csq_rbih_late_war_* cascade may re-author cleansing, forced-displacement, civilian-targeting, hostage-taking, paramilitary-deployment, or any sensitive-act response option. The pragmatic instrumental framework does not relax the canon-gate; the displacement-prohibition stays STRICT on consequence rows.

future_consequences.label: RBiH reintegration offers to Serb/Croat communities (autumn 1993)
future_consequences.explanation: The pragmatic line carries the instrumental dual-track posture (civic rhetoric outward, Bosniak institutions inward) into the autumn-1993 reintegration-offers policy crystallization. The same calculus that drives the Washington Agreement acceptance and the Federation Army integration parallel-commands outcome supports maintain_offensive_posture as the documented historical posture: civic rhetoric outward (the maximalist civic-state claim sustains the moral-high-ground appeal that Silajdžić's UN General Assembly and Washington-London-Bonn shuttle diplomacy is built on); Bosniak institutions inward (no explicit symmetric concession framework toward RS-held communities, since that would surface the dual-track instrumentalism the pragmatic posture relies on staying un-surfaced); the pre-Washington HRHB federation channel kept open as a U.S. shuttle diplomacy track on the Croat side because it is consistent with the dual-track logic (BB Vol. II 1993-94 RBiH diplomatic posture chronology; Izetbegović Inescapable Questions on the autumn-1993 policy crystallization; Silajdžić foreign policy correspondence on the maximalist civic-state external-advocacy framework). The offer_federation_status counterfactual is instrumentally tempting on this branch — it would extend the pre-Washington HRHB channel symmetrically and visibly thread the civic-rhetoric exterior — but the Bosniak-hawks internal_cohesion cost is sharp and risks surfacing the dual-track gap. The conditional_autonomy_proposal counterfactual is the closest pragmatic-line variant — RBiH sovereignty as the precondition preserves both the civic-rhetoric exterior and the institutional inward posture; the international_standing + negotiating_leverage upside is real, the internal_cohesion cost moderated. The accept_de_facto_partition counterfactual collapses the dual-track logic at the constitutional level (territorial_legitimacy -40, military_credibility -25, internal_cohesion -25, international_standing -10) and is structurally inconsistent with both the external and the inward lanes. §3.6 STRICT — this decision is constitutional/diplomatic and no downstream csq_rbih_reintegration_* cascade may re-author cleansing, forced-displacement, civilian-targeting, hostage-taking, paramilitary-deployment, or any sensitive-act response option; the pragmatic instrumental framework does not relax the canon-gate.

RS.headline: Sarajevo affirms civic republic platform
RS.body: The Presidency publicly frames Bosnia as a multi-ethnic republic. Pale reads the statement as an effort to preserve international legitimacy and complicate partition claims.

HRHB.headline: RBiH platform stresses equal citizenship
HRHB.body: Sarajevo's civic line keeps a shared-state option alive on paper. Croat leaders weigh whether the pledge protects local autonomy or masks wartime centralization.

RS.headline: Sarajevo shifts toward national framing
RS.body: The Presidency presents the war in narrower Bosniak national terms. Pale reads the declaration as weakening Sarajevo's civic legitimacy while sharpening the conflict's identity stakes.

HRHB.headline: RBiH deemphasizes civic platform
HRHB.body: Sarajevo's declaration moves away from equal-citizenship language toward a Bosniak national claim. Croat leaders see greater pressure on the alliance and on local autonomy demands.

RS.headline: Sarajevo keeps civic language with narrower practice
RS.body: The Presidency maintains the public vocabulary of a multi-ethnic state while building Bosniak institutions more quietly. Pale assesses a legitimacy strategy with a visible internal gap.

HRHB.headline: RBiH balances civic pledge and wartime institutions
HRHB.body: Sarajevo keeps civic language for diplomacy while consolidating Bosniak wartime structures. Croat leaders can work with the pledge for now, but watch the distance between rhetoric and practice.

historical_source: ICTY Karadzic Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T, 24 March 2016) paras. 32, 48, 50 — Sarajevo Presidency civic-republican platform vs. SDS partition platform. ICJ Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro (Judgment, 26 February 2007) — state-continuity framing of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and recognition timeline. UN A/54/549 (Secretary-General's report on Srebrenica, 15 November 1999) §§ on 1992 Sarajevo posture. ARBiH June 1992 ethnic composition approximately 70% Bosniak, 18% Croat, 12% Serb per Balkan Battlegrounds Vol. I, corroborated by Jovan Divjak (Serb officer serving as ARBiH Main Staff deputy commander).

title: Paramilitary Authorization Policy
narrative: Sarajevo Presidency files. ARBiH command has forwarded a deployment protocol for the irregular formations that emerged in the spring — the Patriotic League cadres, the Green Berets, the Sarajevo-area independent brigades around Caco Topalovic and Celo Delalic, the volunteer detachments forming alongside the 7th Muslim Brigade. The Presidency posture toward integration is in question. The documented Sarajevo position, since the Patriotic League's absorption into ARBiH, has been a single chain of command — irregulars are integrated into regular regiments under ARBiH authority, or they are refused. The political files now require a written posture: refuse the parallel paramilitary track, review each deployment, or authorize the formations on standing orders.

effect.text: The Presidency records a paramilitary deployment policy.

source_note: UN A/54/549 §35 and ICTY Hadzihasanovic/Kubura (IT-01-47) document ARBiH chain-of-command discipline relative to RS and HRHB paramilitary practice. The historical Sarajevo posture was integration of irregulars into the regular army with prosecution of those who refused — the Caco/Celo October 1993 disarming actions are the canonical operational expression of that posture. Sarajevo did not maintain a parallel paramilitary track.
staff_assessment: Refusal mirrors the documented ARBiH integration policy and preserves international standing as legal-conduct evidence at The Hague accumulates. Per-deployment review introduces command friction and slower tempo. Standing authorization is ahistorical for the Presidency and exposes Sarajevo to ICTY-grade scrutiny on the RS/HRHB pattern.
trigger_evidence: The Presidency state-identity platform has been recorded; the irregulars question follows.
ARBiH command has flagged the Patriotic League, Green Berets, and Sarajevo-area independent brigades pending political direction.

response_options.label: Refuse paramilitary deployment
response_options.description: Single chain of command. Irregular formations are integrated into regular ARBiH regiments under Main Staff authority or refused entry to the order of battle. The Patriotic League cadres are absorbed; the Sarajevo-area independent brigades will be brought to heel. International monitors note the posture; the hardline current inside SDA bristles at the constraint.

future_consequences.label: Paramilitary refusal posture recorded
future_consequences.explanation: Refusing the parallel paramilitary track mirrors the documented ARBiH integration policy; international standing rises modestly as legal-conduct evidence accumulates, and internal cohesion takes a small hit reflecting the Caco/Celo-style integration friction with the hardline current.

response_options.label: Review each deployment
response_options.description: Each proposed deployment arrives in the Presidency files with a casualty projection. Regional ARBiH commanders lose blanket authority; the political center retains the decision. Operational tempo slows; the integration line softens; the international monitors note the reviews but reserve judgment until the pattern emerges.

future_consequences.label: Per-deployment modal becomes the player surface
future_consequences.explanation: Per-decision review routes each proposed deployment through a modal with full casualty projection. The csq_paramilitary_authorization_refused counterfactual remains reachable if approvals are never granted; the international-standing penalty remains modest until a deployment is actually approved.

response_options.label: Authorize paramilitary standing orders
response_options.description: Standing authorization. The Patriotic League cadres, the Sarajevo-area independent brigades, the volunteer detachments — all operate on local commander authority without per-mission political review. This breaks with the documented Sarajevo posture. International monitors will read the pattern against Pale and Mostar; the ICTY paper trail will record the policy in its own terms. Each approved sweep records civilian casualties and increments the war-crimes counter through the existing engine surface.

future_consequences.label: Paramilitary sweep engine is the canon-bound consequence surface
future_consequences.explanation: Standing authorization routes paramilitary capture through the existing paramilitary_sweep engine; civilian casualties and war_crimes_events are recorded automatically — not by this option's effects. The international-disillusionment counterfactual becomes reachable on its own flag predicates.

RS.headline: Sarajevo refuses parallel paramilitary track
RS.body: The Presidency formalizes refusal of irregular formations on the ARBiH order of battle. Pale reads the policy as a continuation of Sarajevo's integration line and a deliberate distance from the RS rear-area pattern.

HRHB.headline: RBiH formalizes integration-only paramilitary line
HRHB.body: Sarajevo records refusal of the parallel paramilitary track; irregulars must integrate into ARBiH regiments or stand down. Mostar staff note the contrast with HVO practice and weigh the alliance implications.

RS.headline: Sarajevo introduces per-deployment paramilitary review
RS.body: The Presidency moves from blanket refusal to per-deployment political review. Pale reads the shift as posture signaling rather than a settled break with the integration line.

HRHB.headline: RBiH routes paramilitary requests through political review
HRHB.body: Sarajevo routes each volunteer deployment through Presidency files with a casualty projection. Mostar staff assess slower ARBiH rear-area tempo without a clear repositioning of the integration line.

RS.headline: Sarajevo authorizes paramilitary standing orders
RS.body: The Presidency records standing authorization for irregular formations to operate alongside ARBiH on local-commander authority. Pale reads the choice as a counter-historical departure from the documented Sarajevo posture; the Hague paper trail will record it.

HRHB.headline: RBiH formalizes paramilitary tolerance
HRHB.body: Sarajevo authorizes irregular formations on standing orders. Mostar staff note the policy departs from the documented ARBiH integration line; international standing will compress quickly as the pattern emerges.

historical_source: ICTY Hadzihasanovic and Kubura Trial Judgment (IT-01-47-T, 15 March 2006) — ARBiH 3rd Corps and 7th Muslim Brigade command-responsibility findings establishing the existence and reach of ARBiH chain of command. ICTY Oric Trial and Appeal Judgments (IT-03-68, 30 June 2006 / 3 July 2008) — Srebrenica enclave ARBiH commander; ultimate acquittal on command responsibility in the comparative discipline frame. ICTY Karadzic Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T, 24 March 2016) — comparative narrative on Sarajevo state institutions and chain of command. ICTY Stakic (IT-97-24, 31 July 2003) and Brdjanin (IT-99-36, 1 September 2004) — RS comparator findings on paramilitary tolerance as policy. UN A/54/549 (Secretary-General's report on Srebrenica, 15 November 1999) §35 — Sarajevo posture and chain-of-command institutional context.
